variants.male_north_american: Ryan and Casey had been together four years, and most evenings ended the same way. Ryan came home, sat down at the end of the couch, and scrolled news feeds on his phone until past midnight. Casey said the phone had replaced conversation. Last Tuesday Casey cooked dinner and waited forty minutes while Ryan finished a thread about a factory closing in another state. When Casey finally said something, he answered that it was the only way he could wind down after work, and that being watched made it worse. Casey has started eating alone at the counter. Neither of them has raised it since.

variants.male_north_american: Casey and Ryan shared a one-bedroom apartment where the bedroom was the only quiet room. The argument was about the screen. Ryan read outrage threads in bed with the brightness turned up, some nights until two in the morning, and Casey woke every time the room lit up. Casey asked twice for the phone to stay in the kitchen overnight. Ryan agreed both times, then kept it under his pillow anyway. On Sunday Casey found it there and said the promise had meant nothing. Ryan said he had never promised, only agreed to try, and that Casey was keeping score. Both of them have been sleeping badly.

variants.male_north_american: Ryan was laid off in March and had been applying for work since, with nothing to show for it. Most days he scrolled hiring freezes and layoff announcements from the couch, six or seven hours at a stretch, and had stopped answering messages from friends. Casey said the scrolling was making everything worse and asked him to stop reading the same bad news twice. On Thursday evening Casey unplugged the router without saying anything. Ryan did not speak for the rest of the night. Casey said afterwards that living with him had started to feel like living alone, and that he had not laughed in weeks.
